title: I Made a Big Mistake
reviewNotes: All 53 saved states and narration reviewed. The complete five-piece setup White Ke6/Nb7/d2 versus Black Kc6/g4 is reconstructed. Five branches compare the winning Nd8+/Ke5/Ne6+/Nf4 coordination, drawing Nd6 blockade, premature Nxg2/Kd3, and final Ke3 reserve-tempo cage against ...g1=N. The full main branch retains the win through ...Kb2/d4/Kc3/d5; the source’s ...Kb4/Kf2 alternative also wins. Nf4 is supplied by the saved images where rolling narration skips it. All encoded intermediate positions are checked.
transcript: Anyone can draw a game, but only brave players will dare to push for a win. You see in this position white has an extra knight, but there is this black pawn that it's only three steps away from promoting. So obviously white needs to do something with this knight. Unfortunately, if the knight tries to go to D6, this is actually a draw because despite being able to stop the pawn like this, the black king will keep marching down and overload the knight. And if we try to run the pawn to the defense of the king, black is simply going to promote to a queen distracting the knight and then picking up the pawn drawing the game. So actually, the first incredible move and very counterintuitive that white needs to find is knight to D8. And now of course the black king wants to stay close to the path of the white pawn, so it goes to C5. And white continues by gaining opposition against this king by stepping in front of it. And at the same time, it frees up a new square for the knight. But black is a resilient player and tries to run to the promotion square with G3. So knight E6 is played. The king moves down and it seems like the knight has successfully stopped the pawn. And at the same time, it's preventing the black king from getting closer to our pawn. But there's only an issue. This move doesn't actually stop the pawn because black can simply push. And now the knight is overloaded. Again, if we take this pawn, the black king goes to D3 and it successfully stops the white pawn. So it seems like black is out of the woods, right? Well, not exactly. White plays D3 forcing the king to make a choice, either stepping away from the pawn and allowing us to pick up this pawn and win the game or going to C3. Don't think that this is over yet because if we try to now run to promote our own pawn, black is not simply going to get a queen and allow us to fork it. Instead, black has the brilliant promotion to a knight. And now of course, the fork fails and this, believe it or not, it's actually a draw because the knight is going to be able to sacrifice itself for the last pawn. So in this position, white needs to play king to E4. And now the newly born knight it's actually trapped between the king and the knight. But again, white cannot be hasty because after the black king chases it, we will need to play king E5 to protect the D6 square. Now, this is still going to be a draw. So in this position, the only winning move for white is to keep going down with king E3. Black is actually in zugzwang. Any knight move loses the knight. Now if the king goes down, we simply run with our pawn and there's no way to stop it anymore. And if the king goes up, we simply come here to pick up the trapped knight. If you love incredible chess, follow for more.
